sentences.RES-001.title: Sample ratio mismatch: the arms are not the size the allocation promised
sentences.RES-001.why.1: Random assignment gives arms of the registered sizes, up to chance.
sentences.RES-001.why.2: A mismatch this large means the arms were not formed as designed (a fault in assignment, in logging or in filtering), so who is in each arm may differ and a difference in the metrics can come from that.
sentences.RES-001.why.3: No estimate of the effect can be trusted until the cause is known.
sentences.RES-001.do.2: Find why the counts differ: assignment or bucketing, logging that loses events in one arm, bot or test-account filters, a crash or redirect on one variant, or an exposure rule applied to some arms only.
sentences.RES-001.do.3: The week-by-week table in the evidence shows whether the mismatch began at a point in time.
sentences.RES-001.do.4: Fix the cause and rerun the experiment.
sentences.RES-002.title: Fewer players than the registered sample size
sentences.RES-002.why.1: The registered sample size is what the experiment needs to detect the registered effect with the registered power.
sentences.RES-002.why.2: With fewer players the test has less power than was promised, so a result that is not significant says little about whether the effect exists.
sentences.RES-002.why.3: A design that cannot be sized has no registered sample size at all, so no amount of data meets it.
sentences.RES-002.do.1: Keep the experiment running until every arm reaches its registered n (when the evidence gives sizes, it says how many are missing).
sentences.RES-002.do.2: If it must stop, report the result as underpowered, with the interval of the effect, and not as evidence of no effect.
sentences.RES-002.do.3: Do not lower the registered n after seeing the data.
sentences.RES-002.do.4: If the evidence says the design is unattainable, the spec's baseline and mde_relative cannot be turned into a sample size (the evidence gives the reason): more data will not clear this, so correct them and register the experiment again.
sentences.RES-003.title: Ran for less than the registered minimum duration
sentences.RES-003.why.1: The minimum duration is registered so that the run covers the weekly cycle of behaviour and gives effects that take time to settle a chance to show.
sentences.RES-003.why.2: A shorter run measures a window that may not represent the usual weeks, and cannot show a change over time.
sentences.RES-003.do.1: Run to at least design.min_duration_days, and to a whole number of weeks where you can.
sentences.RES-003.do.2: Do not stop on the day the result looked good.
sentences.RES-003.do.3: If the registered minimum was wrong, say so and why before reading the effect.
sentences.RES-003.do.4: Register design.start_utc: without it the first and last assignment in the export set the duration, and one mistimed row (a timestamp of zero, a default date) can hide this finding.
sentences.RES-004.title: A guardrail is worse than its tolerance allows, or may be
sentences.RES-004.why.1: A guardrail is the registered limit on what a change may cost.
sentences.RES-004.why.2: A change that improves the primary metric and breaks a guardrail has not won on the primary metric alone, and a harm that is real in the sample may be larger or smaller in the population, so a point estimate beyond the tolerance is not the same as a breach.
sentences.RES-004.why.3: Referee therefore separates a breach that is shown (the whole interval is beyond the tolerance) from one that is only possible (the interval still reaches inside it), and reads the harm against control's observed mean, which is the change the experiment caused, and against the registered baseline, which is the spec as written.
sentences.RES-004.why.4: When the two disagree, the stricter decides and the note says which; when control itself is beyond the tolerance of the registered baseline, the baseline may no longer describe the traffic, and a breach against it alone does not show that the arm caused it.
sentences.RES-004.why.5: The intervals are unadjusted for the number of arms and guardrails, so with several of them some will miss, and they take the players to be independent: with a session or a cluster as the unit they are too narrow, which the note says.
sentences.RES-004.why.6: A guardrail within its tolerance is not a finding, and where its interval reaches beyond the tolerance the data cannot rule out a breach.
sentences.RES-004.do.1: Do not decide on the primary metric alone.
sentences.RES-004.do.2: If a shown breach rests only on the registered baseline (the note says which reference decides), or the note says that control itself is beyond the baseline's tolerance, first check whether the baseline still describes this traffic (season, platform mix, a change since it was registered): read the arm against control, and register a new baseline for the next test, not for this one.
sentences.RES-004.do.3: If the reading against control's mean also shows the breach, find what the arm does to the guardrail and either fix it or drop the arm; the tolerance was registered before the data, so do not move it now.
sentences.RES-004.do.4: For a breach that is only possible, the data cannot tell a breach from noise: have the guardrail's owner decide in writing, before the decision, whether the possible harm is acceptable, or run a new registered test of the guardrail with its own sample size, analysed once at its end.
sentences.RES-004.do.5: Do not keep adding players to this test until the interval clears the tolerance: that is another look at the data, the 95% interval does not cover it, and Referee does not adjust for it.
sentences.RES-004.do.6: For a binary guardrail with few events or non-events the interval is rough, and for a revenue-like one it is less reliable than 95% suggests: see the note.
sentences.RES-007.title: The effect differs between cohorts of first exposure, or the test could not run
sentences.RES-007.why.1: The pooled effect is an average over players who were first exposed at different times.
sentences.RES-007.why.2: If the effect differs between those cohorts, the pooled figure describes none of them well, and what a later launch sees can differ from it.
sentences.RES-007.why.3: The test says that the effect differs, not why: a change tied to the calendar week of a cohort (a launch, a promotion, a build, the mix of players acquired) cannot be told from one tied to each player's own time since first exposure, because the export holds seven-day totals only.
sentences.RES-007.why.4: A test that could not run is reported too, so that a missing check cannot read as a pass.
sentences.RES-007.do.1: Read the table of cohorts in the evidence before the pooled effect: each cohort's difference and its standard error on both scales.
sentences.RES-007.do.2: Find out what differed between the weeks of the cohorts (a launch, a promotion, a build, a change in where players come from; RES-013 shows a change of configuration), and report the pooled effect together with the cohort table, naming no cause the data cannot show.
sentences.RES-007.do.3: For existing players, check whether the earliest cohorts are the most active.
sentences.RES-007.do.4: A flag labelled low information is a lead to re-check with more data at the planned end, not a finding.
sentences.RES-007.do.5: If the test did not run, the reason code says what was missing: more traffic or a longer run, arms closer in size, an export made after every outcome window has closed, randomisation and analysis in the same independent unit (player, user or device), or a metric that is not a ratio; for an effect that could not be estimated, values that vary in both arms with a mean above 0.
sentences.RES-007.do.6: The evidence prices the traffic that would let the cohorts be used, from the sizes observed (plans, traffic_needed), says when to export again if the outcome windows of some cohorts had not closed, or says why more traffic would not help.
sentences.RES-008.title: Skewed or heavy-tailed metric: its 95% interval can be wrong more or less often than 5% of the time
sentences.RES-008.why.1: Welch's interval for a difference of means, the one Referee prints, assumes that the mean of each arm is nearly normal.
sentences.RES-008.why.2: For a metric that most players leave at zero and a few drive up, that takes more players than an experiment often has (by the rule of thumb of Kohavi et al., revenue per user, with a skewness of about 18, needs about 114,000 users), and below that size the interval is wrong more or less often than the 5% it states.
sentences.RES-008.why.3: Referee measured how often for a revenue-like metric of independent players in two arms (design section 21.10), and the finding quotes the simulated cases on each side of the comparison: with equal arms the interval was mostly close to or under 5% for a small effect and above it for a large one; with arms of unequal size it was often above 5%, for a small effect mostly on the side that makes the larger arm look better than it is, and it was worst when the control was the larger arm (the arm there being the group with the higher mean); and at 9 to 1 with no effect it was worse the fewer the players who spend in the smaller arm.
sentences.RES-008.why.4: These rates come from one simulated family and are not a measure of the experiment in hand.
sentences.RES-008.why.5: Which simulated effects are read is decided by the difference seen between the two means, which for a heavy-tailed metric is itself noisy: with arms of about equal size an experiment with no effect can read as a warning and one with a large effect as info, and above the largest number of players who spend that was simulated the range of that case is used, which may be a ceiling there.
sentences.RES-008.why.6: A quiet RES-008 is not evidence that the interval is reliable: in the simulations every run of a revenue-like metric showed a sign.
sentences.RES-008.why.7: For a metric that is not revenue-like the finding gives the signs and says that no error rate was measured.
sentences.RES-008.do.1: Where an entry gives a simulated rate, read it in place of 5%: an interval that failed in 10% of simulated experiments behaved like a 90% interval, and for a small effect and arms of unequal size it mostly favoured the larger group.
sentences.RES-008.do.2: Where an entry states no error rate (a metric that is not revenue-like, units that are not independent players, a group with no analysed players, or no player who spends in the smaller group), treat its interval as unchecked: the signs show that it may be unreliable, but Referee has not measured how much.
sentences.RES-008.do.3: Do not call the result significant, or not, on one edge of this interval: if an end of it is close to zero or to a decision threshold, say that the result is uncertain.
sentences.RES-008.do.4: Where you can choose, do not make the control the larger arm, which was the worst case in the simulations (where the arm has the higher mean; for a metric you expect to fall, avoid the larger arm instead), and plan for more players who spend in the smaller arm.
sentences.RES-008.do.5: For a decision that rests on this metric, consider a less skewed version of it (a cap on the amount per player, or a transformation): Kohavi et al. report that capping revenue per user cut its skewness from about 18 to about 5.
sentences.RES-008.do.6: It changes what is estimated, and Referee has not measured how well capping, trimming or a transformation works, so register the choice before the next test and not after seeing the data.
sentences.RES-008.do.7: Referee shows no bootstrap interval, because in its simulations the percentile bootstrap interval failed more often than Welch's in most of the cells it was run on.
sentences.RES-011.title: Sample ratio drifts over time although the total passes
sentences.RES-011.why.1: A mismatch that reverses partway through can cancel in the total, and one that begins or ends partway is diluted in it.
sentences.RES-011.why.2: A failing week points to a change in assignment or logging during the test (a release, a campaign, an outage, a planned ramp-up of the allocation), so the players of that week may not be comparable with the others.
sentences.RES-011.do.1: Find what changed in the failing weeks: a release, a change to assignment or logging, a new traffic source, an outage.
sentences.RES-011.do.2: Decide what to do with those weeks from the cause, never because leaving them out changes the result.
sentences.RES-012.title: Players first exposed after their first purchase
sentences.RES-012.why.1: A purchase made before the player first saw the change cannot be an effect of it.
sentences.RES-012.why.2: These players are left out of the effect analysis, but they are in the arms, so a different share of the exposed players being late in different arms means the change reached the arms differently.
sentences.RES-012.why.3: It is the results-time counterpart of DES-007.
sentences.RES-012.do.2: If it can follow a purchase, say so in the design and analyse from first exposure.
sentences.RES-012.do.3: Compare the estimates with and without these players in the evidence, and say which one the conclusion rests on.
sentences.RES-012.do.4: If the late share differs between arms, find out why before reading the effect.
sentences.RES-013.title: An arm's configuration changed during the test
sentences.RES-013.why.1: A change of configuration part-way through is a second treatment inside the arm.
sentences.RES-013.why.2: Players before and after it saw different things, so the arm's effect is an average of two experiences, and a change of that effect over time (RES-007) cannot be told from the effect of the change itself.
sentences.RES-013.do.1: Find out what changed and when.
sentences.RES-013.do.2: Analyse the versions separately or restart the test on the final configuration; do not pool the versions and read a trend over weeks as novelty.
sentences.RES-013.do.3: The difference within a week in the evidence is descriptive only: the versions were not randomised.
